passages.text: Touchscreen kiosks have made ordering faster for many Koreans, yet they have also shut some customers out. The machines have supplanted cashiers in restaurants, cinemas, and even hospitals, and an order can be modified with a single tap. Older adults and people with visual impairments often find them baffling. Tiny text and cluttered menus bewilder them. Screens set too high for wheelchair users turn a routine purchase into an ordeal. In response, Korea has begun requiring many new kiosks to offer voice guidance and adjustable screen heights. Some local governments also run free classes where seniors can practice ordering on training machines.

Bluetooth is so common that we seldom ask where its odd name originated. In 1997, engineers from several rival firms were collaborating on a short-range radio link that would let phones and computers exchange data without cables. One of them, Jim Kardach of Intel, had been reading a historical novel about the Vikings. He suggested naming the project after Harald Bluetooth, a tenth-century king who had united the Danish tribes. The technology, he argued, would likewise unite competing industries. The name was intended only as a temporary code name, and marketers preferred a blander label. That label, however, could not be registered as a trademark in time. As a result, it was the king's nickname that ended up on billions of devices.

Sea otters live along the coasts of the northern Pacific and are among the few mammals other than primates known to use tools. Floating on their backs, they place a flat stone on their chests and pound shellfish against it until the shells fracture. Unlike most marine mammals, otters lack a thick layer of blubber. Instead, they rely on exceptionally dense fur to keep warm in cold water. They must also eat roughly a quarter of their body weight each day. This voracious appetite benefits the coast because otters devour sea urchins that graze on kelp. Underwater kelp forests can therefore thrive where otters live, which is why biologists have come to regard these animals as a keystone species.

The Scream by the Norwegian artist Edvard Munch is one of the most iconic images in modern art. Munch said the idea came to him during a walk at sunset, when the sky abruptly turned blood red. He sensed an immense scream passing through nature. Rather than paint the scene only once, he revisited it several times in paint and pastel. He also made a print that could be reproduced many times. The best-known painted version from 1893 is housed in the National Museum of Norway. The image has also lured thieves. Two different versions were stolen from Oslo museums in 1994 and 2004. Both were later recovered.

Ordering dinner through a delivery app takes only a few taps, but the meal often arrives encased in far more packaging than food. A single order of soup and side dishes may come in half a dozen plastic containers with their own lids. Disposable spoons and chopsticks usually arrive in yet another plastic bag. The problem is not merely aesthetic, since plastic that escapes collection can clog drains and eventually fragment into microplastics. When delivery orders surged during the pandemic, the containers accumulated in apartment recycling areas. Residents grumbled about the stench.
Recycling them is not as straightforward as it seems. Containers stained with oil or sauce are often too contaminated to be recycled and end up being incinerated or buried instead, while others are made of composite materials that recycling facilities cannot separate.
Several remedies are being tested. Many apps now let customers decline disposable cutlery, which curbs waste at negligible cost. A few cities have experimented with reusable containers that are collected after the meal and washed for the next order. These programs have struggled to entice enough users because returning containers is cumbersome. Experts maintain that even a modest habit such as rinsing containers before recycling them is beneficial. Such inconspicuous steps add up when millions of households repeat them.

For centuries, sailors could gauge how far north or south they were by looking at the sun or stars. They had no dependable way, however, to ascertain their longitude, their position east or west. Navigators relied on dead reckoning, an estimate based on speed, heading, and elapsed time. Its errors compounded over long voyages. Such errors cost ships and lives, so in 1714 the British government offered a lucrative prize to anyone who could resolve the problem.
Many experts expected the answer to come from astronomy by measuring the position of the moon against the stars, a method that demanded careful observation and elaborate tables of calculations. John Harrison, a self-taught carpenter and clockmaker from the north of England, pursued a different approach. He reasoned that a ship could carry a clock set precisely to the time of its home port, and sailors could then compare it with the local time at sea and calculate how far they had traveled. The trouble was that ordinary clocks ran unreliably on rolling ships and in fluctuating temperatures. Harrison devoted decades to building one timepiece after another. His fourth, no bigger than a large pocket watch, kept impeccable time on a voyage to Jamaica in the early 1760s.
Even so, the officials in charge of the prize kept insisting on further trials. Many of them were astronomers. Harrison grew increasingly exasperated as he entered his seventies. Only in 1773, after the king himself took an interest, did the elderly clockmaker receive most of the money he was owed.

Mr. Han's repair stall stood at the corner of our market street between a fish shop and a shoe store. He mended umbrellas mostly, though people also brought him zippers, watch straps, and once a child's broken toy train. Neighbors lingered to chat while he worked, and he dispensed advice as freely as spare buttons. The first time I went there, I carried a flimsy umbrella with two bent ribs and expected him to tell me to buy a new one, as most shopkeepers would have done. Instead, he spread it open on his workbench and scrutinized it as meticulously as a physician examining a patient. "Nothing is ruined just because it is broken," he said as he straightened the metal with a small pair of pliers. It took him ten minutes and cost me the price of a cup of coffee, and I left feeling oddly elated, as though he had salvaged something more precious than an umbrella.
The stall vanished years ago and was replaced by a convenience store. I still cherish that umbrella, though its handle is faded and one panel no longer matches the others. Whenever I am tempted to discard something, I hear his quiet voice and reach for my repair kit instead.

Single-person households now make up about a third of all households in Korea, and businesses have taken notice. Convenience stores sell ready-made meals tailored for one, and supermarkets offer produce in small packs. Many restaurants have added counter seats so that solo diners do not feel self-conscious. Even the housing market is evolving, with more compact apartments and shared buildings that provide communal laundry rooms and kitchens. Surveys indicate that people who live alone tend to spend a larger share of their money on convenience, hobbies, and pets than larger households do. For companies, the implication is clear: products built around the conventional family of four no longer suit a substantial segment of consumers.

Louis Braille was blinded after an accident in his father's workshop in France at the age of three. At a school for blind children in Paris, he learned to read from cumbersome books printed with large raised letters, which were tedious to read and costly to produce. When a former soldier named Charles Barbier visited the school with a code of raised dots devised for passing messages in the dark, the young Braille recognized its potential but also its flaws. By the age of fifteen, he had streamlined the code into a system of six-dot cells that could each be felt with a single fingertip. Today his system is employed by blind readers across the globe.

Hummingbirds live life at high speed. Their wings can flap dozens of times per second, which lets them hover in front of flowers while they sip nectar, and their hearts can beat more than a thousand times a minute during flight. Such exertion burns enormous amounts of energy, so a hummingbird must feed almost incessantly during the day. At night it cannot feed and faces a real risk of running out of fuel. To survive, many hummingbirds enter a deep sleep-like state called torpor. Their body temperature plummets and their heartbeat slows drastically, which substantially reduces the energy they use until morning.

Barcelona's Sagrada Família is renowned both for its astonishing design and for how protracted its construction has been. Construction began in 1882, and the following year a young architect named Antoni Gaudí took over the project. He dedicated the remainder of his life to it and in his final months even lived in his workshop on the site. When Gaudí died in 1926 after being struck by a tram, only a fraction of the church was complete. Work proceeded sluggishly and was financed largely by donations and visitors' tickets rather than by the government. Today cranes still loom beside towers that Gaudí never saw finished.

For most of the twentieth century, cities were designed around the automobile. Homes, offices, and shops were segregated into distinct zones linked by wide roads, and buying groceries often necessitated a drive. A growing number of planners now advocate the opposite approach. The idea of the "15-minute city," promoted by the researcher Carlos Moreno, holds that residents should be able to reach most daily needs, such as schools, clinics, parks, and stores, within a short walk or bike ride from home.
Paris has become the best-known example. Under Mayor Anne Hidalgo, the city has converted some traffic lanes into bike paths, opened school playgrounds to the public on weekends, and planted trees along busy streets. Proponents say walkable neighborhoods curb pollution, foster exercise, and help neighbors get to know one another.
The idea has detractors too. Some shop owners fear losing customers who arrive by car. In several cities, rumors circulated online that the plan would forbid residents from leaving their own districts. Planners have repeatedly refuted this and explain that the objective is to add choices, not to take them away. Critics also worry that walkable districts may become so desirable that rents soar and displace the very residents the plan was meant to serve.

On a mild January day in 1919, a bizarre catastrophe struck Boston's North End. A huge steel tank holding more than eight million liters of molasses, a thick syrup used to make industrial alcohol, abruptly burst open. A brown wave several meters high surged through the streets at a terrifying speed, knocking buildings off their foundations and bending the steel supports of a nearby elevated railway. Twenty-one people were killed and about 150 were injured. As the evening grew colder, the molasses thickened and hampered rescuers who waded through the sticky mass.
Investigators later discovered that the tank had been shoddily built and never adequately tested. Residents had long grumbled that it leaked so badly that local children collected the dripping syrup. Instead of remedying the defect, the company had simply painted the tank brown so that the leaks would be harder to see. After a lengthy lawsuit the company was held liable. The catastrophe also led to stricter regulations requiring qualified engineers to check and approve the plans for large construction projects.

Leafcutter ants, found in the forests of Central and South America, are among the oldest farmers on Earth. Long lines of them can be seen marching along the ground, each ant carrying a piece of leaf much larger than itself. It would be tempting to assume that the ants devour the leaves, but they do not. Instead, they carry the pieces deep into their underground nests, chew them into a soft paste, and use it to feed a special fungus that grows in large gardens. The fungus in turn yields nourishment that the ants and their young eat.
They began this kind of farming millions of years before humans planted their first crops. Like human farmers, they must safeguard their gardens from pests. Some of the ants harbor beneficial bacteria on their bodies that produce chemicals which prevent harmful molds from overrunning the fungus. Researchers have even studied these chemicals in the hope of discovering new antibiotics. A large colony can contain millions of ants divided by size into distinct roles. Tiny workers tend the garden while large soldiers guard the nest. Collectively, a single colony can strip an astonishing amount of vegetation from the surrounding forest.

During the pandemic, many people were confined at home for long months, and sales of houseplants soared in Korea and many other countries. For some owners, the plants became more than ornaments. They christened them, chatted to them, and fretted when the leaves turned yellow. The term "companion plant" has since become commonplace, and some local governments, including Seoul's, have even opened clinics where residents can bring ailing plants for diagnosis and advice. Researchers posit that tending a living thing, even a silent one, can instill a sense of routine and purpose. For those who live in solitude or cannot keep pets, a plant on the windowsill may be a modest but meaningful companion.

The word robot is now ubiquitous, from factory floors to science fiction, but it originated on a theater stage. In 1920 the Czech writer Karel Čapek finished a play about a factory that manufactures artificial workers. He first intended to call these beings by a word based on the Latin for labor, but it struck him as too scholarly. According to Čapek, his brother Josef, a painter, suggested robot instead, a word drawn from the Czech robota, meaning forced labor. When the play was staged in London and New York in the early 1920s, the new word traveled with it. Within a few years it had permeated many languages around the world.

The pistol shrimp is only a few centimeters long, yet it is one of the noisiest creatures in the sea. One of its two claws is much larger than the other and can snap shut at astonishing velocity. The snap propels a jet of water so rapidly that it forms a minute bubble. When the bubble implodes a moment later, it emits a sharp crack and a burst of heat that briefly reaches thousands of degrees. The shock is potent enough to stun or even kill small fish and crabs, which the shrimp then devours. Intriguingly, the noise does not stem from the claw striking itself but from the collapsing bubble.

The Mona Lisa is now the most visited painting in the Louvre, but it was not always so celebrated. In August 1911 it vanished from the museum. The thief was Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian handyman who had once worked at the Louvre. He concealed himself inside the building, removed the painting from the wall, and strolled out with it under his garments. According to most accounts, the painting stayed hidden in his room in Paris for more than two years. Meanwhile, newspapers everywhere covered the mystery and throngs came to gaze at the vacant space. In 1913 Peruggia attempted to sell the painting to an art dealer in Florence and was apprehended. By then the Mona Lisa had become a global celebrity.

Local festivals have become a lifeline for many small towns in Korea. Virtually every region now hosts one, celebrating anything from cherry blossoms and butterflies to local foods such as crab and ginseng. For towns with dwindling populations, a thriving festival can attract tens of thousands of visitors in a single weekend, filling restaurants and guesthouses that are deserted the rest of the year.
Success has its drawbacks, however. In recent years, visitors have posted photos online of exorbitantly priced food at some festivals, such as a small plate of grilled pork that cost as much as a full meal at an upscale restaurant. Such posts circulate rapidly, and a single complaint can tarnish a festival's reputation for years. In response, some towns began to disclose food prices in advance and to inspect stalls during the event.
Experts also observe that many festivals look alike, with the same food trucks, singers, and souvenirs. They urge towns to concentrate on what makes their area distinctive, whether it is a local craft, a historic site, or a dish found nowhere else. Such features give visitors an incentive to return.

The colors of autumn leaves come from a quiet chemical change inside them. During spring and summer, leaves are saturated with chlorophyll, the green pigment that plants use to convert sunlight into nourishment. Chlorophyll is so abundant that it masks other pigments in the leaf, including yellow and orange ones called carotenoids. As the days grow shorter and cooler, trees prepare to shed their leaves for winter. They cease producing new chlorophyll and break down what remains, reclaiming valuable nutrients before the leaves fall. With the green gone, the hidden yellows and oranges finally emerge.
Reds and purples are a separate matter. These colors come from pigments called anthocyanins, which many trees actually synthesize in autumn rather than simply reveal. Scientists are still debating why a tree would expend energy manufacturing new pigments in leaves it is about to lose. One hypothesis is that the pigments function like sunscreen and protect the leaf while the tree extracts nutrients from it. Sunny days and cool nights tend to yield the most vivid reds, which is one reason autumn colors fluctuate from year to year.

My grandmother sold vegetables from a folding table at the edge of the morning market. On Saturdays she let me take charge of the money box. It was a battered cookie tin, and inside it she kept coins arranged in paper cups. Her customers were mostly elderly neighbors who seldom bargained, and some lingered to gossip. I was proud of my quick arithmetic, so the first time a customer handed me a large bill, I calculated the change mentally and dropped it into his palm without a word. Grandmother remained silent until he had gone. Then she demonstrated her own method, placing each coin and note into the customer's hand one at a time and counting up aloud from the price to the amount paid. "It is not about whether you are right," she said. "It is about letting them see that you are honest."
I have worked in offices for two decades now, and I seldom handle cash. But whenever I submit a report or an invoice to a client, I strive to show my work step by step, the way she counted coins into a stranger's hand.

Choose the word that most appropriately completes the dialogue.
A: Did the manager say anything about the report you handed in two days late?
B: Not much. She was quite ____ about it and only asked me to be on time next month.
늦은 보고서에 대해 다음 달엔 제때 내라고만 했다는 뒷말이 단서라 '너그러운(lenient)'이 맞아요. nimble(재빠른)·archaic(낡은)·sterile(불모의)는 사람이 일을 대하는 태도와 이어지지 않아요.

Choose the word that most appropriately completes the dialogue.
A: Your roommate practices the drums every night? That must drive you crazy.
B: Yeah, it really does ____ me. I can hardly sleep before midnight.
A 의 drive you crazy(미치게 하다)를 B 가 Yeah 로 받아 바꿔 말한 자리라 '몹시 짜증 나게 하다(exasperate)'가 맞아요. recoup(되찾다)·certify(증명하다)·replenish(다시 채우다)는 소음과 관계없어요.

Choose the word that most appropriately completes the dialogue.
A: The taxi driver charged us double the usual fare last night. That's way too much.
B: I know. The fare was simply ____; next time we're taking the bus.
A 의 way too much(너무 비싸다)를 I know 로 받아 고쳐 말했으니 '터무니없이 비싼(exorbitant)'이 맞아요. pliable(유연한)·taciturn(과묵한)·intangible(만질 수 없는)은 요금을 꾸미지 못해요.

Choose the word that most appropriately completes the dialogue.
A: You're still studying for that certification exam? You never give up, do you?
B: Right. My sister keeps urging me to ____, and I'm still at it.
A 의 never give up(포기하지 않다)을 Right 로 받아 바꿔 말한 자리라 '끈질기게 계속하다(persist)'가 맞아요. encrypt(암호화하다)·calibrate(눈금을 맞추다)·swaddle(포대기로 싸다)는 공부와 이어지지 않아요.

Choose the word that most appropriately completes the dialogue.
A: You must have been really nervous before the job interview yesterday.
B: Oh, yes. I was full of ____ the whole morning before it started.
A 의 really nervous(몹시 긴장한)를 Oh, yes 로 받아 고쳐 말했으니 '두려움, 불안(trepidation)'이 맞아요. remittance(송금)·verbiage(군말)·posterity(후손)은 마음 상태가 아니에요.

Choose the word that most appropriately completes the dialogue.
A: Should we tell the new neighbors that their dog barks all night?
B: Yes, and let's be ____ of their feelings when we do. They just moved in.
be ____ of their feelings 짝이 단서예요. considerate of(~을 배려하는)로 이어지고, 이사 온 지 얼마 안 됐다는 뒷말과도 맞아요. frigid(몹시 추운)·extant(현존하는)·legible(읽을 수 있는)은 feelings 와 짝이 되지 않아요.

Choose the word that most appropriately completes the dialogue.
A: Is everyone in your group actually doing their share of the project?
B: Not really. One member keeps finding excuses to ____ his duties, and the rest of us cover for him.
his duties 를 목적어로 받는 짝이 단서예요. 핑계를 대며 맡은 일을 '피하다(dodge)'가 맞아요. ripen(익다)·exhale(숨을 내쉬다)·consecrate(신성하게 하다)는 duties 와 짝이 되지 않아요.

Choose the word that most appropriately completes the dialogue.
A: The forecast for Saturday looks dismal. Maybe we should go hiking another day.
B: Agreed. Let's ____ the trip until next weekend.
A 의 another day(다른 날에)를 Agreed 로 받아 바꿔 말한 자리라 '미루다(defer)'가 맞아요. laminate(코팅하다)·abduct(납치하다)·extort(갈취하다)는 여행 일정과 관계없어요.

Choose the word that most appropriately completes the dialogue.
A: The CEO's speech this morning lasted barely two minutes, didn't it?
B: Yes, it was very ____, and it still covered everything that mattered.
A 의 barely two minutes(2분도 안 되는)를 Yes 로 받아 고쳐 말했으니 '간결한(concise)'이 맞아요. hereditary(유전의)·indigenous(토착의)·populous(인구가 많은)은 연설을 꾸미지 못해요.

Choose the word that most appropriately completes the dialogue.
A: Are Minho and Jisu still not talking after their quarrel last month?
B: Actually, they finally ____ last week. They're even planning a trip together.
함께 여행을 계획한다는 뒷말이 단서라 다툰 두 사람이 '화해했다(reconciled)'가 맞아요. evacuated(대피했다)·appraised(감정했다)·conscripted(징집했다)는 다툼 뒤의 일과 이어지지 않아요.

Choose the word that most appropriately fills in the blank.
Because the evidence against him was so ____, the jury needed less than an hour to reach a guilty verdict.
Because 와 so 뒤 '한 시간도 안 걸려 유죄 평결'이 결과라, 증거가 '설득력 있는(compelling)' 것이었어요. pliable(유연한)·laconic(말수 적은)·febrile(열이 나는)은 증거를 꾸미지 못해요.

Choose the word that most appropriately fills in the blank.
To ____ the irate customers, the new manager offered every table a free meal and a written apology.
To 부정사가 목적이고, 화난 손님에게 무료 식사와 사과문을 건넸으니 '달래다(placate)'가 맞아요. revamp(개편하다)·foreshadow(예고하다)·salvage(건져 내다)는 손님을 목적어로 받는 뜻이 아니에요.

Choose the word that most appropriately fills in the blank.
Although critics disregarded the painter during her lifetime, her works are now considered ____ and have shaped generations of artists.
Although 로 살아서 무시당한 것과 대비되고, 여러 세대 화가에게 영향을 주었으니 '새 흐름을 연(seminal)'이 맞아요. tepid(미지근한)·queasy(메스꺼운)·prosodic(운율의)는 작품 평가로 이어지지 않아요.

Choose the word that most appropriately fills in the blank.
The senator refused to ____ the details of the agreement, keeping them confidential until both sides had signed it.
keeping them confidential(비밀로 두다)이 앞말을 고쳐 말한 것이라, 내용을 '밝히기(divulge)'를 거부했다가 맞아요. hoist(들어 올리다)·sow(씨를 뿌리다)·pluck(뽑다)는 details 와 이어지지 않아요.

Choose the word that most appropriately fills in the blank.
Doctors recommend regular exercise to ____ the symptoms of mild depression, along with professional treatment.
to 부정사가 운동의 목적이라 증상을 '누그러뜨리다(mitigate)'가 맞아요. tantalize(애태우다)·anoint(기름을 붓다)·devolve(넘겨주다)는 symptoms 와 짝이 되지 않아요.

Choose the word that most appropriately fills in the blank.
The hikers took a ____ route around the lake, a long, winding detour that added two hours to their trip.
쉼표 뒤 a long, winding detour(길고 구불구불한 우회로)가 빈칸을 고쳐 말한 것이라 '빙 돌아가는(circuitous)'이 맞아요. nonchalant(태연한)·solicitous(걱정하는)·superlative(최상의)는 길을 꾸미는 말이 아니에요.

Choose the word that most appropriately fills in the blank.
The entrepreneur's start was ____: a small garage, two employees, and a single borrowed table saw.
쌍점 뒤 작은 차고, 직원 둘, 빌린 톱 하나가 빈칸을 풀어 쓴 것이라 '보잘것없는(modest)'이 맞아요. spurious(가짜의)·tacit(암묵적인)·salubrious(건강에 좋은)은 그 목록과 이어지지 않아요.

Choose the word that most appropriately fills in the blank.
Marine biologists warn that coral reefs are highly ____ to even slight increases in water temperature.
____ to 짝과 warn 이 단서라 '~에 영향받기 쉬운(susceptible to)'이 맞아요. taciturn(과묵한)·thrifty(검소한)·placid(차분한)은 to 와 짝을 이루어 수온 변화와 이어지지 않아요.

Choose the word that most appropriately fills in the blank.
The author's earlier books were so ____ that only specialists could follow their arguments.
so ~ that 뒤 '전문가만 따라갈 수 있었다'가 결과라 '난해한(abstruse)'이 맞아요. congenial(마음 맞는)·lukewarm(미지근한)·hardy(강인한)은 읽기 어려움의 까닭이 되지 않아요.

Choose the word that most appropriately fills in the blank.
Many residents publicly ____ the highway plan as a threat to the area's last green space.
decry A as B(A를 B라며 비난하다) 짝이 단서예요. 마지막 녹지를 위협한다고 했으니 '공공연히 비난했다(decried)'가 맞아요. whittled(깎았다)·outsourced(외주를 주었다)·sequestered(격리했다)는 as a threat 와 짝이 되지 않아요.
